name: exact-fails-is-not-mathlib-lacks-it
description: I built a lemma because exact? offered only a universe-stuck suggestion; the goal closed by inferInstance, because the fact ships as an instance
metadata:

---

I needed "a subsingleton module is flat". `exact?` returned only
`Module.Flat.of_shrink`, whose universe parameters it could not infer, so I wrote
`Module.Flat.of_subsingleton'` by hand via a `LinearEquiv` to `PUnit` — and
documented "absent from mathlib as a usable lemma", citing the `exact?` failure as
the measurement. An audit closed the same goal with plain `inferInstance`: mathlib
has `Module.Free.of_subsingleton` as a `priority := 100` **instance**, so `Flat`
follows by synthesis, cross-universe. My hand-rolled version was also strictly
weaker — it pinned `R` and `M` to the same universe.

**Why:** `exact?` searches for a *term* by unifying lemma conclusions; it does not
run the instance graph on the goal the way `infer_instance` does. So for any goal
that is a **class**, an `exact?` failure measures the lemma index, not
derivability. The two instruments answer different questions and I quoted the wrong
one as evidence of absence.

**How to apply:** before building a brick for a class-valued goal, try
`infer_instance` / `inferInstance` — not just `exact?` / `apply?`. If `exact?`
returns something universe-stuck, that is a hint the fact exists as an instance
under a different name, not that it is missing. Then check the **use site**: mine
closed by `inferInstance` there too, which is the check that would have caught it.

Sibling of [[failing-inferinstance-is-not-absence]] and
[[failed-inferinstance-vs-named-theorem]] — those say a failed `inferInstance` does
not prove absence; this is the converse direction, and both reduce to: name the
instrument, and match it to whether the goal is a class or a term.

Related: [[failing-exact-on-composite-goal]], [[cited-instance-one-wrapper-away]].

---
name: stale-lock-makes-commit-hang
description: A zero-byte index.lock makes git commit HANG, not fail; commit-tree + update-ref bypasses it and is compare-and-swap safe
metadata:
  type: project
---

The shared ledger at `.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git` carried a **zero-byte
`index.lock`** on 2026-07-30. Effect: `git commit` did not error — it **hung**. My
call timed out at 2 minutes having written the tree, with the ref never moved, and
the only visible symptom was the `diff --cached` output appearing and then nothing.
Easy to misread as "the commit landed".

The fix, which also removes a race the private-index recipe does not:

```sh
TREE=$($G write-tree)
PARENT=$($G rev-parse HEAD)
C=$($G commit-tree "$TREE" -p "$PARENT" -F msgfile)
$G update-ref refs/heads/<branch> "$C" "$PARENT"   # <- compare-and-swap
```

The third argument to `update-ref` is the expected old value, so the write fails
loudly if another lane moved HEAD in between — strictly better than `commit`, which
writes the whole index and can clobber. Do **not** delete the lock: other lanes may
be relying on it (see the workspace's own I-1504).

**Two things to check after every commit**, both of which caught real problems for
me in one session:
- `git diff --name-status HEAD~1 HEAD` on your **own** commit. An **empty stat**
  means another lane's integrate sweep already banked your file — your work is in
  the tree carrying *their* message, with nothing explaining it.
- HEAD-vs-disk `sha256sum` on every path you touched.

Related: [[read-tree-commit-race]], [[postcommit-stat-and-head-hash-are-both-needed]],
[[uncommitted-work-reaches-head-via-other-lanes]], [[commit-with-pathspec-not-index]].
